analysis.one_liner: Offers Senate candidates public campaign funding in exchange for running on small-dollar donations.
analysis.headline: Thirty senators — 28 Democrats and 2 independents — backed the bill, but the Senate Finance Committee never held a hearing or a vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a voluntary program where Senate candidates can qualify for public campaign money by collecting many small contributions ($5 to $150) from residents of their own state. Participating candidates then receive lump-sum allocations, a six-fold match on small-dollar donations, and discounted TV ad vouchers — in exchange for giving up large contributions and their own money. The fund would be paid for by a 0.5% tax on payments under federal contracts worth more than $10 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates willing to run without big checks: they qualify by gathering at least 2,000 contributions of $5–$150 from state residents, then get a base allocation ($750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district), a 600% match on small-dollar donations, and broadcast ad vouchers. Ordinary voters gain candidates who are not financed by large donors, plus cheaper ads, more debates, and better disclosure of ad purchases.

how_it_helps.text: Participating candidates receive a lump-sum allocation of at least $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district, plus a 600% match on small-dollar contributions from state residents.
To qualify, a candidate must collect at least 2,000 contributions of $5 to $150 each from residents of their own state, replacing large checks with broad small-donor support.
The program would be paid for by a 0.5% tax on payments under federal government contracts worth more than $10 million, capped at $500,000 per contract per year.

Participating candidates get broadcast ad vouchers and pay no more than 80% of the lowest unit rate for television airtime, and stations must give candidates the same terms as their most favored advertisers.
Individuals get a refundable tax credit covering 50% of up to $50 in contributions to Senate candidates, and participants must take part in at least one primary and two general-election debates.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors with contracts over $10 million pay a 0.5% excise tax on those payments, which contractors may partly pass through into contract prices. Large donors and big-money committees lose their outsized access to Senate candidates who join the program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large federal contractors and big donors

drawbacks.text: The program is voluntary: candidates who stay out face no restrictions, and independent spending is untouched, so outside money could still swamp publicly funded campaigns.
The 0.5% contractor tax may be passed into the price of government contracts, so taxpayers could partly bear the program's cost indirectly.
The tax itself is only a 'sense of the Senate'; the fund still depends on Congress appropriating the revenue each year, so it could be underfunded by future Congresses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gain — Senate campaigns funded by broad small donations instead of large checks from interests with business before Congress — is large and the direct cost is modest: a half-percent levy on big contracts, capped per contract. The main design weakness is that the program cannot compel participation or reach independent spending, so its effect depends on how many candidates and parties opt in.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Fair Elections Now Act on July 26, 2017, with 25 original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced — its only action beyond introduction.
The bill ended the Congress with 30 cosponsors: 28 Democrats and 2 independents, and no Republicans.
The committee never reported the bill, and the Senate never debated or voted on it before the Congress expired on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the large donors, party committees, and major contractors whose money finances Senate campaigns — the existing financing system, with all its large-check dependence, stayed in place. The bill's small-dollar alternative never got a test.

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Elections Now Act and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 30 senators.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill referred to his committee.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote.

against.name: Broadcasters
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed expanding the lowest-unit-charge rule and political ad rate requirements that this bill would extend and tighten.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats (28) or independents (2); not one Republican signed on, and Republicans who chaired the Finance Committee and ran the Senate majority took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Companies with contracts over $10 million would pay a 0.5% tax on those payments to fund the Fair Elections Fund. The same companies are among the biggest campaign contributors, so the bill's financing mechanism doubles as a check on their political influence.

industries.industry: Large political donors and party fundraising committees
industries.note: Participating candidates would accept only small contributions and fund allocations, and joint fundraising committees — the vehicle for six- and seven-figure checks — would be barred for them. Wealthy donors lose their leverage over any senator who joins.

Stations would have to accept public vouchers and sell airtime to participating candidates at up to 20% below the lowest unit rate, cutting margins on political ads; vouchers also guarantee general-election ad revenue. Political advertising is among broadcasters' highest-margin inventory.
